# 2 Chronicles 6:1–21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

This chapter is the prayer of dedication for Solomon’s temple. It closely parallels 1 Kings 8:12–53, though verse 13 (the bronze platform) is unique to Chronicles. The Pulpit Commentary divides the chapter into Solomon’s remarks to the assembly (vv. 1–11) and his prayer to God (vv. 12–42). The prayer itself — the longest recorded in Scripture at 28 verses — opens with praise (vv. 14–15), then three petitions: perpetuate David’s line (v. 16), regard the place of the Name (vv. 17–20), and hear prayers made toward this place (v. 21), followed by seven specific cases.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## Verses 1–2 — Solomon acknowledges God’s dwelling in the cloud and the temple

**v. 1:** *“Then Solomon declared: ‘The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick cloud…’”*

Solomon’s opening words are prompted by the Shekinah glory cloud that had just filled the temple (2 Chron 5:13–14). JFB notes this cloud was “a densely opaque and uniformly shaped cloud descending in a slow and majestic manner” — the recognized symbol of divine presence throughout Israel’s history (Ex 19:9; 24:16; 40:34; Lev 16:2; Num 9:15). Solomon “referred not to any particular declaration of God, but to the cloud having been all along…the recognized symbol of the divine presence.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-chronicles-6.html

The Pulpit Commentary adds that God’s glory being veiled in “clouds and darkness” (Ps 97:2) is “essentially what he ever has said and ever is doing in all time…it is a fact and it is necessary that his glory be for the present veiled.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

Precept Austin notes the LXX uses *kataskenoo* for “dwell” — literally “to pitch one’s tent,” suggesting permanent settlement. The thick cloud is the Shekinah glory cloud.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

**v. 2:** *“…and I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.”*

The Pulpit Commentary says “for ever” refers “rather to the permanence and stationariness of the temple as the dwelling-place of the ark…than design any prophecy of length of time. They contrast with the wandering people, and wandering worship and sacrifices, and wandering tent and tabernacle.” David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that Solomon “rightly sensed that the presence of the cloud meant that God dwelt in the temple in a special way. As long as this did not slip into a superstitious misunderstanding, it was good to recognize a special place to come and meet with God.” He quotes Selman: “Though only Jesus is God incarnate, the temple was a clear sign that God in all his being was committed to living among his people.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

---

## Verses 3–6 — Solomon blesses the assembly and blesses God

**v. 3:** *“…the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel…”*

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Solomon had been facing the symbol of God’s presence (the temple/cloud) when speaking vv. 1–2, and now “faces round to the assembly.” The exact words of blessing are not recorded here; the Pulpit Commentary suggests the blessing may be “wrapt up tacitly” in what follows (v. 4), or perhaps 1 Kings 8:55–61 preserves its substance.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

**v. 4:** *“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has fulfilled with His own hand what He spoke with His mouth to my father David…”*

David Guzik says Solomon recognized “that the temple was the fulfillment of God’s plan, not David’s or Solomon’s. David and Solomon were human instruments, but the work was God’s.” He quotes Selman: “The mention of God’s hands (lit. ‘fulfilled with his hands’) really means that God’s actions have confirmed his words — it is as if God’s unseen hands were active in all the human hands who contributed to the construction work (cf. 1 Chronicles 29:16).”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

The Pulpit Commentary observes that expressions like “with His hands…with His mouth” show “how language formed itself in the concrete mould at first” — the antithesis between God’s speaking organ and His acting organ is a Hebrew idiom for faithful fulfillment.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

Precept Austin notes: Frederick Mabie comments that “Solomon’s temple-dedication prayer begins with expressions of praise and thanksgiving that focus on God’s faithfulness to fulfill his promise to David.” J.A. Thompson adds that for the Chronicler, “the building of the temple and the establishment of the Davidic dynasty as a consequence of the divine promise was the important focus.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

**vv. 5–6:** God’s election of Jerusalem and David. God had not chosen any city or permanent ruler since the Exodus — the tabernacle wandered and leaders were temporary — “but now I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there, and I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.”

The Pulpit Commentary explains: “The tabernacle and all it contained had but travelled from place to place…and from Moses’ time all the leaders of the people Israel had been men in whom vested no permanent and no intrinsic authority.” Verse 6 marks the decisive divine election.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

Precept Austin cites Andrew Konkel on the significance of “Name” — “Name indicates possession; in the Amarna letters it is an idiom for ownership. Just as the Pharaoh owned Jerusalem by placing his name there, so the Lord now owns the temple and all that it represents.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

---

## Verses 7–11 — David’s desire, God’s redirection, and fulfillment

**vv. 7–9:** David’s heart desired to build the temple. God commended the desire — “you have done well to have this in your heart” — but assigned the actual building to Solomon.

David Guzik notes: “It confirms that David’s disqualification was not due to sin, but because the concept of God’s rest must be regarded as the unique and final stage in building the temple” (quoting Selman). David prepared extensively but “was happy for the credit and honor for building it to go to his son Solomon.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

Matthew Henry (cited in Precept Austin) observes: “Temple-work is often thus done; one sows and another reaps (Jn. 4:37, 38), one age begins that which the next brings to perfection. And let not the wisest of men think it any disparagement to them to pursue the good designs which those that went before them have laid.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

**vv. 10–11:** Solomon declares God has fulfilled His word: Solomon sits on David’s throne and has built the temple, and placed the ark — containing the covenant — within it.

The Pulpit Commentary remarks on vv. 10–11: “The moment that might have witnessed the utmost inflation of spiritual pride…is saved from the peril. To the ‘performing of the Lord’ the glory is all given (Luke 1:54, 55, 68–72). Probably delivered from earthly feeling…Solomon was in a very high degree ‘in the spirit’ (Rev 1:10) on this great day.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

JFB notes that Solomon here “refers to himself the divine promise made to his father (cf. 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Chronicles 22:9, with 2 Samuel 7:23–29).”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-chronicles-6.html

David Guzik: “Solomon recognized that his succession of David on the throne of Israel was a significant thing. He was the first king to follow his father as a hereditary monarch.” The ark was “the chief glory of the temple…a representation of God’s covenantal presence with His people.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

---

## Verses 12–13 — Solomon’s posture: the bronze platform

**v. 12:** *“Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.”*

The Pulpit Commentary notes Solomon stood (and later knelt) eastward of the altar, facing the temple and congregation: “Although the voice of Solomon was raised in prayer to God, yet the prayer was to be that of the whole congregation and not of priestly proxy, and therefore of the whole congregation it must be heard.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

David Guzik: “Solomon did not dedicate the temple from within the temple. It would be inappropriate for him to do so because he was a king and not a priest.” Spreading out hands “was the most common posture of prayer in the Old Testament…a gesture of surrender, openness, and ready reception.” Guzik also quotes Spurgeon: “It is worthy of remark concerning this prayer that it is as full and comprehensive as if it were meant to be the summary of all future prayers offered in the temple.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**v. 13:** *The bronze platform* — unique to Chronicles (absent from 1 Kings 8). Five cubits long × five cubits wide × three cubits high (approx. 7.5 × 7.5 × 4.5 ft), placed in the middle of the courtyard. Solomon stood on it, knelt, and spread his hands toward heaven.

JFB notes the Hebrew word for “scaffold” (*kiyyor*) is the same word used for “laver” (basin) elsewhere (18 of 21 occurrences). This “suggests the idea that this throne might bear some resemblance, in form or structure, to those lavers in the temple, being a sort of round and elevated pulpit.” JFB adds: “It is deserving of notice that there was no seat in this pulpit — for the king either stood or knelt all the time he was in it.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-chronicles-6.html

The Pulpit Commentary confirms the same Hebrew word *kiyyor* is translated elsewhere as “laver” (18×), “pan” (1×), “hearth” (1×), and here “scaffold” — suggesting “the stand was in some sort basin-shaped.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

The Biblical Illustrator (cited in the search results on v. 18) captures the spirit of this moment: “Never was Solomon so exalted, never was he nearer heaven, than when on bended knees we behold him a suppliant at the footstool of God’s throne. The highest rank, the loftiest genius, the most splendid crown, receive a double splendour from the grace of humility.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## Verses 14–15 — Opening praise: God’s uniqueness and covenant faithfulness

**v. 14:** *“O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth, keeping Your covenant of loving devotion with Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts.”*

David Guzik: “Solomon recognized that God was completely unique. The pretended gods of the nations could not compare to Him in any way.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

The Pulpit Commentary notes that “the quoting of Scripture and the utilizing of language in which the religious feeling of those who have gone before has expressed itself had plainly set in” — Solomon draws on Exodus 15:11–12 and Deuteronomy 7:9.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

The structure identified by the Pulpit Commentary: vv. 14–15 are the two-verse opening of the great prayer, followed by three petitions.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

**v. 15:** *“You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David. What You spoke with Your mouth You have fulfilled with Your hand this day.”*

David Guzik: “Solomon first thanked and praised God for His past fulfillment of promises.” This mirrors v. 4 — what God spoke with His mouth, He fulfilled with His hand.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

Precept Austin includes a related devotional: “In a world of uncertainty, our trust is in a faithful God who will always keep His promises.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

---

## Verses 16–17 — Petition: Perpetuate the Davidic line

**v. 16:** *“Therefore now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, what You promised…‘You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your descendants guard their way to walk in My law…’”*

David Guzik calls this “the great secret to power in prayer — to take God’s promises to heart in faith, and then boldly and reverently call upon Him to fulfill the promises.” He quotes Spurgeon: “God sent the promise on purpose to be used…nothing pleases God better than to see his promises put in circulation; he loves to see his children bring them up to him, and say, ‘LORD, do as thou hast said.’” Guzik adds: “Just because God promises does not mean that we possess. Through believing prayer like this, God promises and we appropriate. If we don’t appropriate in faith, God’s promise is left unclaimed.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

The Pulpit Commentary cross-references 2 Samuel 7:12; 1 Kings 2:4; 6:12; and Psalm 132:12 for the conditional element: “yet so that thy children take heed to their way.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

**v. 17:** *“And now, O LORD, God of Israel, please confirm what You promised to Your servant David.”*

The Pulpit Commentary cross-references 1 Chronicles 17:9–13. The Hebrew expression is “let thy word be verified.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## Verses 18–21 — The great theological centre: God’s transcendence and immanence, and the plea for God’s attention

**v. 18:** *“But will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.”*

This is the theological high point. David Guzik says: “We are glad that Solomon said this. From prior statements, such as his statement in 2 Chronicles 6:1-2, we might have thought that Solomon drifted towards a superstitious idea that God actually lived in the temple to the exclusion of other places. It was important to recognize that though God had a special presence in the temple, He was far too great to be restricted to the temple.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

The Pulpit Commentary notes: “Solomon’s conception of the infinite God comes plainly to view here (2 Chronicles 2:6; Deuteronomy 10:14; Psalms 139:5–12; 148:4; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:49; Acts 17:24).”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

The Biblical Illustrator develops this extensively: “I. A FALSE THOUGHT OF GOD IN RELATION TO THE SANCTUARY… Solomon had no such false thought about Jehovah; he knew that ‘the heaven of heavens could not contain him’… God’s presence is not to be limited in our thought in any way whatever. He is ‘within no walls confined.’” Yet “II. THE TRUE THOUGHT OF HIM IN THAT RELATION. As those who worship God in the sanctuary, we should accustom our minds to think of him as: 1. The very present One. ‘Will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth?’ In very deed and in truth. Not only is his presence everywhere…but he is actively present there, interested in all that is passing there.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/2-chronicles-6.html

J.A. Thompson (cited by Precept Austin) comments: “This small structure in Jerusalem…was the place where divine transcendence and divine immanence would meet. On the one hand, no building, not even the whole earth, could contain God…On the other hand, in some special way God would be here, in this temple, more than in any other place. Perhaps this helps us understand the mystery of the incarnation of God in Christ — while God fills the whole universe, he also is specially present in the person of Christ.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

Martin Selman (cited by Precept Austin): “The theme of God’s dual residence cascades through the chapter, without ever being logically resolved. It is enough to know that God lives on earth as well as in heaven.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

JFB: “No person who entertains just and exalted views of the spiritual nature of the Divine Being will suppose that he can raise a temple for the habitation of Deity as a man builds a house for himself…Solomon described the true and proper use of the temple, when he entreated that the Lord ‘would hearken unto the supplications of His servant and His people Israel, which they should make toward this place.’”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-chronicles-6.html

**v. 19:** *“Yet regard the prayer and plea of Your servant, O LORD my God, so that You may hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You.”*

Despite God’s transcendence, Solomon presses his plea for God to “regard” (*panah* — turn toward) his prayer. The Pulpit Commentary notes the earnestness of this request — that “prayer may be heard.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

**v. 20:** *“May Your eyes be open toward this temple day and night, toward the place where You said You would put Your Name…”*

The Pulpit Commentary cross-references Exodus 29:43; Deuteronomy 12:5; 14:23; 15:20; 16:2 for the Deuteronomic theme of “the place where the LORD chooses to put His Name.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

David Guzik notes: “Solomon asked God to incline His ear towards the king and the people when they prayed from the temple. For this reason, many observant Jews still pray facing the direction of the site of the temple in Jerusalem.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**v. 21:** *“Hear the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive.”*

The Pulpit Commentary cites Professor James G. Murphy: “The great thought of Solomon now is that the centre and core of all worship is prayer.” The phrase “from heaven, Your dwelling place” distinguishes God’s true heavenly dwelling from the temple — 1 Kings 8:30 reads “hear to thy dwelling-place, to heaven,” which the Pulpit Commentary suggests may involve a copyist’s variation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

David Guzik: “Solomon knew that the most important thing Israel needed was forgiveness. This was the greatest answer to prayer Israel could expect from God.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

## Denominational and Other Perspectives

Given the constraints of my searches, here is what I could find regarding tradition-specific readings:

### Baptist / Evangelical (Spurgeon tradition)

David Guzik’s commentary (Enduring Word, widely used across evangelical and charismatic circles) repeatedly cites Charles Spurgeon, a Reformed Baptist. Spurgeon’s key emphases include: (a) the prayer as “as full and comprehensive as if it were meant to be the summary of all future prayers offered in the temple”; (b) the language being “full of quotations from the Pentateuch…the sense of the whole may be found in those memorable passages in Leviticus and Deuteronomy”; (c) the principle of “using” God’s promises in prayer — “God sent the promise on purpose to be used…nothing pleases God better than to see his promises put in circulation.” This reflects a classic Baptist emphasis on taking God at His word and pleading His promises in prayer.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

### Reformed / Presbyterian

The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary (a standard Reformed reference) emphasizes the theological precision of Solomon’s statements — particularly that God is not contained in any building, and that the true purpose of the temple was not housing Deity but providing a place for prayer and worship according to the Mosaic dispensation. JFB also highlights the covenant-historical dimension: Solomon refers the divine promise made to David to himself.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/2-chronicles-6.html

### Methodist / Holiness

Matthew Henry (widely used across Methodist and Reformed traditions, cited by Precept Austin) emphasizes the moral and devotional application: that Solomon did not build in pride but for God’s glory; that “temple-work” passes across generations; that God commends good intentions even when He redirects their fulfillment. Henry’s emphasis on purity of motive and humble dependence fits the Holiness tradition’s concern with the heart.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

David Guzik’s Enduring Word commentary, while broadly evangelical, is used in many Pentecostal and charismatic settings. The emphasis on the Shekinah glory cloud, the physical postures of prayer (spread hands, kneeling), and the “missionary impulse” behind Solomon’s prayer for foreigners all resonate with charismatic emphases on God’s manifest presence, embodied worship, and global mission. Guzik’s stress on “appropriating” God’s promises through faith-filled prayer is also characteristic.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

### Modern Scholarship

Andrew Konkel (cited by Precept Austin) explains that in the ancient Near East, kings built or refurbished temples “as an affirmation of the god that enabled their rule. David was denied this assurance, but in its place he received a divine promise now fulfilled.” The “Name” theology reflects Amarna-era idiom where placing one’s name signified ownership.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

Martin Selman (likewise cited) emphasizes the unresolved tension between God’s heavenly dwelling and earthly presence — “The theme of God’s dual residence cascades through the chapter, without ever being logically resolved.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

J.A. Thompson notes the Chronicler’s distinctive emphasis: “In Solomon’s address to the assembly he was stressing the fulfillment of God’s promise to David more than the exodus. The building of the temple and the establishment of the Davidic dynasty as a consequence of the divine promise was the important focus for the Chronicler (cf. 1 Chr 17).”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

### Catholic and Orthodox

I was unable to reach the Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sites within my search/fetch limits for specific commentary on this passage. The Haydock Catholic Commentary is listed among the resources at StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-6.html) but I could not fetch it. Based on known Catholic exegesis, the temple is typically read typologically as prefiguring both Christ’s body (John 2:21) and the Church as the dwelling-place of God — an approach already hinted at by J.A. Thompson and the Biblical Illustrator in the sources above.

---

## Key Themes Running Through the Passage (from the sources consulted)

1. **God’s transcendence and immanence held together** — God dwells in thick darkness, heaven cannot contain Him, yet He chooses to place His Name in the temple (Pulpit, Guzik, Selman, Thompson).
2. **Covenant faithfulness** — the temple fulfills the Davidic promise; God’s spoken word and acting hand are one (JFB, Pulpit, Guzik).
3. **Prayer as the core of worship** — the temple is primarily a house of prayer, not a container for Deity (Pulpit citing Murphy, JFB, Guzik).
4. **Forgiveness as the greatest need** — Solomon’s first and foundational plea is “hear and forgive” (Guzik, Pulpit).
5. **The conditional nature of the Davidic promise** — “if only your descendants guard their way” (Pulpit, Guzik).
6. **Praying God’s promises back to Him** — the model of taking God’s own words and reverently asking Him to fulfill them (Spurgeon via Guzik).
